title: Saturday for Mary
hookLine: many Catholics give Saturdays to Mary

cards: Ask an older Catholic what Friday is for, and you may hear about fish. For centuries Friday was a day without meat, kept in memory of the cross, and Catholics are still asked to mark it with some small penance.

Sunday belongs to the resurrection. That leaves the day in between, the one that so often goes to laundry and errands. In many Catholic homes and parishes, by an old and quiet custom, Saturday belongs to Mary.

teach.b: Nobody can point to the day this began. The custom grew slowly in the monasteries of the early Middle Ages.
Alcuin of York, a scholar at Charlemagne's court around the year 800, is often credited with writing votive Masses for each day of the week, and he gave Saturday to Mary.
Within a few centuries the Saturday Mass of Our Lady was common across Europe. Why Saturday? The sources don't settle it, but one answer has stuck.
Think of Holy Saturday. Jesus lies in the tomb; the disciples have scattered and gone into hiding; the Gospels say almost nothing about that day.

Tradition pictures Mary as the one who kept faith while everything was silent, waiting for Sunday. So every Saturday, the eve of every Sunday, is a small echo of that waiting. Luke gives her a habit that fits.
After the shepherds leave Bethlehem, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart."
Kept and pondered: a Saturday kind of faith.

teach.h: A MEMORIAL STILL IN THE CALENDAR.
teach.b: The custom is still in the Roman calendar. On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when no other memorial falls, a parish may keep the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday.
In 1925 Sister Lúcia, one of the three Fatima children, said Mary had asked for a devotion of five first Saturdays: confession, Communion, the rosary and fifteen minutes of meditation.

teach.h: MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS, PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.
teach.b: Many parishes still keep it. At home, the simplest way is the rosary, or even one decade of it. It's a custom, not a law, and not every Catholic keeps it.
But it gives the week a shape: the cross, the waiting, the morning.

how: Many Catholics pray the rosary or a Marian prayer on Saturdays; on free Saturdays in Ordinary Time a parish may celebrate the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday, and some keep the Fatima devotion of the five first Saturdays.

games.q: it's the Saturday after the crucifixion. the disciples have scattered and gone into hiding. what does tradition picture Mary doing?
o: keeping faith and waiting for Sunday.
going to the tomb to roll away the stone.
games.why: the Gospels are nearly silent, but tradition pictures her keeping faith while everything was quiet. that's one reason Saturday became hers.

practice: If you pray the rosary, take one decade slowly: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be, and let your fingers keep count so your mind doesn't have to.
If you don't pray, or don't have beads, take ten slow breaths, and with each one bring back one thing from this week you'd like to keep and ponder, the way Luke says Mary did.

wordCard.voice: votive Mass. A Mass offered for a special intention rather than the day's usual one; Alcuin of York is credited with writing one for each day, giving Saturday to Mary. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Saint Mary on Saturday — the name of the Saturday memorial.

carryVoice: Your line: saturday is hers. A quiet day, kept with her, before the morning comes. Day six hundred ninety-two, done.
